News.title: At least 30 dead in horror stampede at popular tourist hotspot with ‘many young people’ feared to be among victims
News.content:
DISASTER ZONE At least 30 dead in horror stampede at popular tourist hotspot with ‘many young people’ feared to be among victims

AT LEAST 30 people have been killed in a horror stampede at a holiday hotspot in the Caribbean, with many students feared to be among the dead.

The fatal crush happened at packed tourist attraction, Laferriere Citadel in northern Haiti.



Haiti’s PM Alix Didier Fils-Aime confirmed “many young people” were visiting the tourist site when the tragedy unfolded.

News.title: Boy, 15, shot in Birmingham park as cops launch manhunt for gunman & appeal for CCTV
News.content:
SHOOTING HORROR Boy, 15, shot in Birmingham park as cops launch manhunt for gunman & appeal for CCTV

A 15-YEAR-OLD boy was rushed to hospital after being shot in a park – with police launching a manhunt for the gunman.

Paramedics were called to Ward End Park in Birmingham just before 10pm on Friday (April 10).





Armed officers are understood to have been scrambled to the scene and initially gave the boy first aid.

The teenager – found near the Foxton Road entrance – was taken to hospital with gunshot wounds, where he remains in a stable condition, according to West Midlands Police.

His injuries are not believed to be life threatening.



Our Major Crime Unit (MCU) is investigating, including the review of CCTV in and around the park.

Detective Superintendent Ryan Chambers, from our MCU, said: “This appears to be an isolated incident and there will be an increased police presence in the area to assist with the investigation and reassure the community.”

We are appealing to anyone who was in the area or may have witnessed the incident, to get in touch with us.

You can do so via Live Chat on our website or by calling 101 quoting log 5589 of April 10.

News.title: US and Iran FAIL to agree peace deal as talks break down after 21 hours in Pakistan leaving fragile ceasefire on brink
News.content:
JD VANCE has blasted Iran for refusing to accept Donald Trump’s “simple proposal” for peace after 21 hours of crunch talks failed.

The vice president said he offered the regime a final and best offer but they refused, as both delegations quickly left Pakistan empty handed in the early hours of Sunday morning.





Vance – who led the US delegation – added: “So we go back to the United States, having not come to an agreement.”

The main sticking point during the lengthy talks came due to Iran’s refusal to halt their nuclear ambitions, the US said.

Vance told reporters as he boarded Air Force Two to leave Islamabad: “Do we see a fundamental commitment of will for the Iranians not to develop a nuclear weapon… for the long term?

“We haven’t seen that yet.”

American negotiators insisted they were flexible and accommodating across the peace attempts.

A Pakistani source said there were “mood swings” from both sides with the temperature shifting “up and down” throughout the meeting.

There remains slim hope of the fragile ceasefire currently in place extending.



Vance concluded: “We leave here with a very simple proposal; a method of understanding that is our final and best offer.

“We’ll see if the Iranians accept it.”

Iranian negotiators left Pakistan shortly after Vance announced the failed talks.

Iran’s foreign ministry said the talks were conducted in an atmosphere of “mistrust”, and called on Washington to refrain from “excessive demands and unlawful requests”.



The regime blamed the US for collapsing negotiations.

Fars News Agency quoted one source as saying: “The Americans demanded through negotiations everything they could not obtain through war.”

They added that the main disagreements came over nuclear technology and the Strait of Hormuz, which has been blocked off by Iran since the start of the conflict.

A source close to the negotiators believed “the American team was looking for an excuse to leave the negotiating table”.

Israel have weighed in on the discussion with security cabinet minister Zeev Elkin saying more talks are still an option, but warned: “The Iranians are playing with fire.”



The two-week ceasefire agreed on Tuesday began after Trump vowed to unleash a “civilisation-ending blitz” on Iran if the regime refused terms to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

It remains unclear if attacks on Iran will resume while a reopening of the vital waterway now appears to be off the table.

It comes after US officials revealed the withering regime has stalled reopening the vital shipping lane because it cannot locate the mines it planted.



As Vance left Pakistan with no deal, Trump was spotted in Miami watching a UFC cage fight.

It was unclear whether the US president knew negotiations had failed by the time he entered the arena for the event.

But Vance said he had spoken to the US president several times during the course of the discussions.

On his way to Florida Trump had told reporters it did not matter to him if a deal was reached.

“We win regardless”, he said. Adding: “We’ve defeated them militarily.”



On Saturday, Trump declared he is now “clearing out” the Strait of Hormuz to allow for global trade to pass through the key waterway again.

The US president said the heavily-mined strait would be safe to pass again soon as in a show of strength he ordered two US Navy destroyers to travel across through the vital shipping lane as the make-or-break summit began.

The risky move – the first time US warships have crossed the strait since the start of the six-week war – was reportedly carried out without Iran’s knowledge.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Tehran later called it a violation of the fragile two-week ceasefire deal.

A US official said the bold move was designed to encourage the globe that ships can begin to pass the commercial shipping and break Iran’s iron grip on the route.

News.title: Labour urged to tackle crisis of jobless young people by cutting hiring costs
News.content:
LABOUR is being urged to tackle the crisis of jobless young people by cutting hiring costs.

Tax rises are making it hard for firms to employ them, according to MPs.





Higher minimum wages, National Insurance hikes and employment rights changes are hitting businesses.

The number of NEETs — young people not in education, employment or training — is close to a million.

Tory Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said: “Builders are desperate to hire [young people] but Labour have piled on costs that make it too expensive to give them a chance.

“You don’t fix youth unemployment by taxing the jobs they need. If we want our kids earning, we’ve got to cut the costs and stop pricing young people out of work.”



Reform’s Lee Anderson said: “All Labour has been successful at is destroying the job market while young people struggle to get a foot on the ladder.”

The Sun on Sunday’s Builder Better Britain campaign has helped secure youngsters placements in construction trades.

A Government spokesman said: “This Government inherited a dire shortage of construction workers and is determined to deliver more opportunities.

“That’s why our youth employment support package, totalling £2.5billion, includes the offer of £2,000 for each new employee aged 16 to 24 taken on by a small business, supporting almost one million young people and delivering up to 500,000 opportunities to earn and learn.”



They said those hiring under-21s earning below a certain level do not pay NI contributions.

News.title: Britain is at its weakest in 400 years – we need to prioritise bullets over benefits, Kemi Badenoch warns Starmer
News.content:
KEMI Badenoch has warned Britain is at its weakest in 400 years — as she pledged to go on the biggest ever peacetime rearming blitz.

The Tory leader said the UK has been “prioritising benefits over bullets” and is facing a day of reckoning.





Unleashing both ­barrels on PM Sir Keir Starmer, she branded his failure to find the billions needed to fund our military “a national disgrace”.

And she accused the Government of lying by ­pretending we are prepared for war, adding: “We are not ready.”

Ms Badenoch was speaking at the London Defence Conference, where she set out her plan to ramp up defence spending.

It came as the US and Iran held the first day of peace talks in Pakistan.



She said President Donald Trump had doled out some uncomfortable home truths — that Britain “cannot properly defend ourselves” without the US.

She said: “It is the culmination of long-standing policy failures which have left our defence capabilities arguably at their weakest in 400 years.

“I don’t need to tell you how this happened.

“Between 1989 and 2022, defence spending fell every year.



“We have grown fat on welfare. Prioritising benefits over bullets.”

The war in Iran exposed our shortcomings — with the UK unable to even send a warship to the region as missiles rained down on our allies and bases, she added.

Ms Badenoch said: “For a proud nation used to stamping its ­influence on the world, Britain’s lack of ­readiness for this war in Iran has been shocking.

“We weren’t just unprepared ­militarily, with no Royal Navy ­warships in the Middle East for the first time in decades. We were strategically unprepared too.”

Blame for this lies with the PM and not our brave Royal Navy, the Tory leader claimed.



She said Sir Keir has been too busy U-turning on benefits and caving to his rebellious backbenchers to prepare for war.

She said: “We have a Government that was politically unprepared for this war, distracted by its own infighting and psychodrama.

“The war in the Gulf must act as a wake-up call. Not for navel ­gazing or finger pointing about who did what, but for action.”

The Government-commissioned strategic defence review, co-authored by General Sir Richard Barrons, was published last year.

It set out the urgent rearming programme needed to make the UK war-ready.



But the Government has still not published the investment plan ­setting out how it will pay for higher defence spending.

Ms Badenoch branded this delay a “national scandal” and added: “Our Government literally doesn’t have a plan.”

Laying out her alternative defence spending blueprint, she promised to cut welfare and Net Zero projects to pay for weapons.

She said: “The next Conservative Government would reinstate the two-child benefit cap and spend that money on defence.

“That will fund the largest net increase in British troops under any Government since the Second World War. We will use the money to recruit 6,000 regular soldiers and 14,000 reservists — as well as paying for their accommodation and equipment.



“And we will reallocate £17billion from Government R&D [research and development work] and Ed Miliband’s disastrous Net Zero ­projects to create a new ­Sovereign Defence Fund.”

In a direct plea to the PM, she said the Tories will put party politics aside and unite with Labour to find cash for defence spending.

She said: “Let’s find the money to rearm. Let’s identify the ­spending cuts.

“And if we reach agreement on a joint plan, Conservatives will ­support those measures in ­Parliament on a three-line whip.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But No10 hit out at the ­Conservative leader’s offer.



A Downing Street spokeswoman said: “Kemi Badenoch sat around the Cabinet table when the Conservatives hollowed-out our Armed Forces. We have announced the biggest uplift in defence spending since the Cold War

“We won’t be taking any advice from her.”

News.title: Construction industry is crying out for young labourers… but Govt policies have priced youngsters out of jobs
News.content:
Shameful waste of Britain’s young

IT IS a national disgrace that a million youngsters are sitting on the scrapheap.

Nearly 13 per cent of all 16 to 24-year-olds are not in education or employment.



What makes this disaster even worse is that the construction industry is crying out for young labourers.



The Government’s ludicrously ambitious target of building 1.5million new homes by 2029 already looks like falling short by as much as a third.

Building firms need a quarter of a million new workers, like the youngsters we took to sites across the UK this week to get work experience.

So why can’t bosses plug their own gap and take 250k youngsters off the dole at the same time?

Because of the Government’s own ruinous policies of course.



They have priced youngsters out of jobs and tied employers in knots of red tape.

Under Labour’s increased minimum wage, firms simply can’t afford to train young people and the apprentice scheme is a sprawling mess.

This double failure is shameful.

It lets down a generation of youngsters who want to work but are confined to welfare, some for the rest of their lives.



And it is blocking the vital housing programme Britain so desperately needs.

Sir Keir Starmer is keen to trumpet the importance of Labour values.

What value is there in allowing this shambles to continue?

How many chances?

ANYONE who thinks our broken justice system is a recent phenomenon should study the insane case of rapist Neil Trennan.

This monster was first jailed for life in 1990 when he raped a woman after attacking her with a dumb-bell.



Yet in 2002 he was allowed day release, escaped from his supervisor and launched a sexually motivated attack on another woman, receiving a second life sentence.

In any normal system that would be enough to prevent him ever receiving leniency again.

But not in the opinion of the Parole Board, who recommended him for an open prison in 2023.

Astonishingly this fiend, who admitted he was addicted to sexual violence, was then allowed out on unsupervised day release, during which he absconded and tried to rape a third woman.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The judge who handed him a third life sentence in February is absolutely right to demand Justice Secretary David Lammy immediately investigate this outrage.



Mr Lammy must identify those responsible for letting this sex beast roam free and kick them out of the justice system.

News.title: Cruel words about late Queen are shameful and unnecessary – but evil specimen Andrew has made her an easy target
News.content:
IT is less than four years since the longest-reigning monarch in British history died.

But how quickly memories fade.



During that short time, some have forgotten all the good Queen Elizabeth II did during her 70 years on the throne.

They are also overlooking the respect she still deserves.

A new profile on her has been written in the (once!) respected Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, which is supposed to serve as a record of our notable public figures.



But it resembles something your average Gen Zer would put on TikTok.

It says the UK “ceased to be a great power in the world” under her.

It claims she adapted “slowly and not always enthusiastically” as Britain evolved into “a multicultural, multi-faith, multi-ethnic society”.

The biased anti-royalists wrote that she “had not been born to succeed” but by her “example, her self-discipline, her public spiritedness, and her longevity, she did so in more ways than one, living out perhaps the most remarkable life of her times.”

It makes her sound like a bigoted old aunt, forced into a job she didn’t want, but we just kind of tolerated her because she stuck around for so long.



This couldn’t be further from the truth. She was respected, loved and admired.

So many of the words seem cruel and unnecessary.

They have also chastised her “mis-steps” (particularly in relation to her family). And maybe here lies the real problem: Andrew.

Because of this vile specimen, who denies any wrongdoing, she has become an easy target. But just like us, the Queen didn’t know the truth before her death.

You don’t have to like the monarch to write about her.



But if you’re compiling her national biography profile, you should really make it your business to know what her role entailed.

A constitutional monarch serves as the ceremonial head of state.

Yes, the Prime Minister consults the monarch — and she would encourage and warn — but she didn’t make the political decisions that shape this country.

She graciously, invisibly, guided 15 Prime Ministers from the wings. (And how unsteady things have come without her presence.) This stabilising figure also urged, over many decades, people to embrace diversity, cultures, faiths and the Commonwealth.

As her job was to guide, not to tell us what to do, I am not quite sure how “enthusiastic” the authors of this barbed biography expected her to be.



Sense of duty

Her work was tireless, with 21,000 royal engagements in all.

She made friends along the way, from Nelson Mandela to comedian Billy Connolly, and showed her own great sense of humour in sketches with James Bond for the Olympic Games, with Paddington for her Jubilee.

She supported grandson Harry’s Invictus Games.

During Covid she remained strong and stabilising, telling us: “We will be with our friends again; we will be with our families again; we will meet again.”

She always led by example, always had a sense of duty.



Even at her husband’s funeral, when she sat alone to adhere to Covid distancing regulations.

We will never forget that haunting image of her with a black mask covering her pale face and just those glistening eyes visible above.

Our hearts went out to the nation’s grandmother and we wanted to console her.

Now is our chance to support her again.

Because so many of us do.



Half the country watched her funeral when she died.

And this month, as we celebrate what would have been her 100th birthday, let’s all pay our respects again.

Spread the positive truth about this great monarch to our own grandchildren so they hear about her from us, not that shameful biography.

We must cherish her great memory, not desecrate it.

I’M LOVING ANGEL’S EVERLASTING LOOK

THERE was a time when your granny looked, well, old. But how times have changed.



When Kate Jackson, Jaclyn Smith and Cheryl Ladd celebrated 50 years of TV show Charlie’s Angels this week, they could have passed for women decades younger. Especially Jaclyn.

She’s 80 and old enough to be my mother but could easily pass as my sister.

She maintains her ageless looks with a healthy lifestyle and diet, a good skin care routine and perhaps the key is that she uses her “own fat” for facial enhancement.



If that’s all it takes, lucky her. I’m all for a few tweakments when my credit card allows.

Now Jaclyn has become a pensioner influencer, other women might also want to hurtle towards an aesthetics clinic after collecting their bus pass.

But there’s only so much nipping and pricking you can do without looking ridiculous.

And Jaclyn has something most of us have never had – natural supermodel beauty, with flawless skin and cheekbones to die for.

She wouldn’t have got to say “Good morning” to Charlie for five years without those genes.



GROW UP, YOU BRATS

WHAT a disappointing pair of brats Sydney Sweeney and Zendaya have turned into.

They were once firm friends but Sydney is said to have flirted with Zendaya’s “is-he-isn’t-he-hubby” Tom Holland and they are also suffering from some sort of career rivalry.

But their career is acting – their current job is promoting their raunchy show Euphoria, and putting on a red-carpet performance is part of the job description.



Maybe they should have remembered that and acted like professional grown-ups, rather than refusing to even stand on it together at the premiere.

lTHERE is a strange new illness spreading around the pet world.

A study in the Netherlands has found that cat and dog owners are making false claims that their animals are sick – or even harming them – to seek attention from vets.

The majority of clinics there are familiar with the phenomenon.

The RSPCA says it’s also happening here despite huge vet bills.



These people have more money than sense.

READY, OR NOT

I’VE started a new health kick and it’s all thanks to Watford businessman Stephen Akuoko.

After reading about how he kept fish in a bath next his toilet before cooking them into ready-meals, I’ve gone right off convenience food.



All meals will now be cooked from scratch.

EGG ON THEIR FACES

IF you’ve been asked to look after something important by your boss that’s, say, priceless or even a collector’s piece, or for example a Faberge egg and watch set valued at up to £2.2million, what would you do with them to keep them safe?

A) Put them in an actual safe.



B) Keep them under your pillow.

C) Shove them in your bag and pop to the packed Dog and Duck pub in London’s Soho.

Oddly, Rosie Dawson opted for C.

Rosie was supposed to be guarding the Faberge items after taking them for display at a work event for her employers at the Craft Irish Whiskey Company.

But in the pub she put the bag down to greet a friend and quick-thinking thief Enzo Conticello swiped it – and its high-value goodies.



He flogged the lot to buy drugs and has been jailed for 27 months.

During his sentence he was told the theft had caused “inconvenience and stress” to Rosie and her company.

I imagine they all needed a stiff drink to get over that loss.

CHOC & CAW

STARS seemed to align last Sunday.

The weather in Manchester was good, I didn’t hit snooze on the 5.30am alarm, and hid chocolate all over my garden.



But 90 minutes later, when my seven-year-old went out with his basket, many of the foil-wrapped chocolate figures had disappeared.

It took a hunt of my own on our security camera to find the culprit . . . a great big thieving magpie.

Hope he was sick.

WHEN Greek prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis announced he was banning social media for teens to tackle anxiety and sleep problems, he added that “many of the younger ones among you will be angry with me”.

Now, yes, but they will thank him one day.

News.title: Sadiq Khan has to wake up… horror on Primrose Hill shows London I love is teetering on the edge of lawlessness
News.content:
IF Britain was not stark raving mad, we’d be honouring Walker Smith today.

Mr Smith, 54, tackled a shoplifter in Waitrose, his place of work for the last 17 years.



The man should have got a medal. Instead, he got the sack.

Because when Walker Smith saw some lowlife stuffing her bag with multiple Lindt Gold Bunny Easter eggs that she had not paid for, he intervened.

“I’ve seen it happen every hour of every day for the last five years,” he said.



“It’s everybody, from drug addicts to teenagers, nicking bits and bobs or walking out with bottles of wine in their arms. We’re not allowed to do anything.”

The cops, the courts and our political masters do not give a toss about shoplifting. But Walker Smith cared.

And caring cost this principled, decent man his job.

I have seen Mr Smith described as a security guard but that is incorrect. Walker was a shop assistant.

Security had been scaled back — “Because shoplifting incidents aren’t reported enough” — leaving non-security staff like Walker on the front line of the shoplifting plague.



So how can his employer imagine that he is the bad guy?

“There is a serious danger to life in tackling shoplifters,” simpered a witless Waitrose spokesperson.

“And that’s why we have policies in place that must be strictly followed.”

In other words — let the thieving bastards get away with it.

And Sir Sadiq Khan, Labour Mayor of London, has the brass neck to insist that the capital is “a safe city”.



Sadiq’s unconvincing evidence?

The cold comfort of knowing that London has a lower murder rate than “every state in the USA”.

As if having a lower homicide rate than gun-mad, psycho-stuffed America was a reason to break out the bubbly.

“Unfortunately, London-bashing has become something of a national and international sport with populist politicians, commentators and keyboard warriors trading in fear, not facts,” sighed Sadiq.

“We should be proud of how safe London is,” echoes Sir Mark Rowley, Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police.



But in the first few weeks of spring, horrific crimes have occurred all over the capital.

On Primrose Hill during a sunny afternoon, a 21-year-old man was stabbed to death.

Finbar Sullivan had taken his new camera — a 21st birthday present — to Primrose Hill to take some photographs. Finbar never came home.

Here was a gentle, creative young man who did his best to steer clear of trouble.

“When he got a scooter, he would ride to school and it would take him ages because he would avoid all the areas where there were gangs,” said Finbar’s heartbroken father, Chris Sullivan.



“He did not wear black because of that — he didn’t want to be associated with any gangs. He wore pale colours.”

Finbar knew all the dangers. It did not save him.

Just five days earlier, Eghosa Ogbebor was shot dead in Woolwich — another murder in broad daylight. Eghosa was 14.

In Golders Green, Jewish ambulances were firebombed.

And in Clapham, a mob of youths ran riot, ransacking shops and terrifying families.



And there is one reason for this social breakdown. There are far too many scumbags out there who believe that they are going to get away with their crime.

From shoplifting to carrying — and using — a deadly weapon.

From stealing Easter eggs to stealing phones to stealing some innocent boy’s life.

Running riot

Behind every single one of these crimes I guarantee that there is someone who thinks that they will never be punished.

Take your head out of the sand, Mr Mayor. Wake up and smell the sewer that our beloved London is becoming, Sir Mark.



This week the Met showed off its new fleet of armoured vehicles, £180,000 nine-tonne monsters called SandCats.

The money would have been better spent putting more old-school coppers on the street.

Because we desperately need a mayor who can see the heart-wrenching reality of crime running riot in the capital. We need cops who care, laws that bite, courts that are capable of making the scumbags fear that they will be punished.

The London I love is teetering on the edge of total lawlessness.



Sacked by Waitrose, Walker Smith has been offered a job by Lord Richard Walker, the boss of Iceland.

Lord Walker wants security guards to carry truncheons and pepper spray to fight shoplifting — that cosy euphemism for retail theft.

In Sainsbury’s, some security guards have been issued stab vests.

Costa Coffee has started having bouncers on the door across the capital to guard fridges.

Stab vests in Sainsbury’s! Bouncers in coffee shops!



There is not one worker in a London supermarket who does not feel that they are in mortal danger every day they go to work.

And Sadiq Khan complacently assures us London is a safe city?

Mr Mayor, you are out of your tiny mind.

Sydney to join the Q

HOLLYWOOD director Paul Feig suggests Sydney Sweeney should be the next James Bond.



“There have been some cool Bond girls,” says Paul, who directed El Syd in domestic thriller The Housemaid. “But come on! Let her be the super-spy. She’s great.”

Seems a bit of a long shot. But when Sweeney was once asked if she fancied being a Bond girl, she retorted: “I think I would have more fun as James Bond.”

She was not kidding. The Housemaid was shot for a reported $35million and has made about $399 million worldwide.

Which makes Sweeney the hottest star in Tinseltown. Could she really be the next 007?

With those kinds of figures at the box office, Sydney Sweeney can be whatever she likes.



WHEN they flew around the far side of the moon, the astronauts on Artemis II ventured deeper into space than anyone has ever been – 252,760 miles from Planet Earth.

An extraordinary moment for humanity.

And despite the calm, smiling competence of the crew, they were putting their lives at risk for every second.

The most memorable moment of my childhood was gazing up at the moon in the summer of 1969 and knowing that humans were walking on its surface. Isn’t it glorious to be back?

Trump fuels EU fans



THERE is a theory that Donald Trump is driving the UK back into the arms of the European Union. You can see the logic.

Most of us do not mind if the POTUS is rude about our socialist Prime Minister. We can’t stand him either.

But all of us feel our blood boil when the President is abusive about British Armed Forces.

In January Trump sneered that in Afghanistan – where the UK had 457 military deaths and thousands of our brave men and women suffered life- changing injuries – frightened Nato troops stayed “a little off the front line”.

Trump quickly retracted that lie. But his sneering has never really stopped. This President is too quick to casually call us cowards.



And disgustingly chummy with Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

A YouGov poll revealed that only 14 per cent of British people still believe we have a “special relationship” with America, 57 per cent want to get closer to the EU.

And if the European Union was smart, it would be wooing this country, and welcoming us back with open arms.

But it is not smart.

Watch the appetite for Rejoining shrivel when we contemplate the real cost. Finally giving up the pound for the euro.



Throwing open our borders and learning to love the Schengen Area.

Forgetting about the budget rebate negotiated by Margaret Thatcher.

And above all, bitterly regretting the error of our Brexit-voting ways and begging Europe for forgiveness.

This is what will stop us ever going back inside the EU. Brussels will want us to crawl.

Cheers Philip A NEW book, Queen Elizabeth II, by Hugo Vickers, describes in vivid detail the last night of Prince Philip’s life. Vickers reports that Philip “gave his nurses the slip, shuffled along the corridor on his Zimmer frame and helped himself to a beer”. The next morning the Duke quietly slipped away after a bath. He was 99 years old. That’s the way to go.

JOANNA LUMLEY, 79, joined a neighbour in confronting a gang of bikers attempting to steal her car from outside her home in Stockwell, South London.



The gang fled empty-handed when they saw the glint in Joanna’s eyes.

Which is possibly a bit of a surprise if you only know Lumley as pie-eye fashionista Patsy in Absolutely Fabulous.

But if you first saw her as karate-chopping, butt-kicking Purdey in The New Avengers, then it was totally in character.

I bet pet soon Fritz in with Heidi’s hubby

HEIDI KLUM steps out in New York with a mystery companion – a Yorkshire terrier mix called Fritz, who is from a pop-up adoption centre next to where the model and TV host was working.



“It took some convincing with my husband,” confesses Heidi.

Heidi’s husband will come around.

It is always the family member who is most resistant to the idea of getting a dog who falls most deeply in love with his new four-legged roommate.

News.title: DWP benefits alert over payments for people with this health condition
News.content:
DWP benefits alert over payments for people with this health condition

MPs discussed proposals to improve access to DWP benefits

View Image You may want to check if you can claim more DWP benefits (Image: Getty)

MPs have spoken about proposals to enhance access to DWP benefits. People may want to do a quick check to see if they can claim any more Government support, in light of the discussion.

‌



Various payments are available from the DWP, including Universal Credit and PIP (Personal Independence Payment) for those of working age, or Pension Credit and Attendance Allowance for those of state pension age. The Treasury Committee recently consulted with policy advocates about efforts to expand access to the benefits system. Discussions centred on the Government's Financial Inclusion Strategy, a policy aimed at boosting financial engagement and awareness of the support available to people.

‌



Helen Undy, chief executive of the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute, which was founded by financial journalist Martin Lewis, highlighted a crucial omission from the strategy. She said: "The bit that could have gone in this strategy that is missing is around how you address the £24billion a year of unclaimed benefits-that figure is from Policy in Practice."

‌



State Pensioners to face major tax change

Financially excluded

She added: "We should be talking about how we increase access to income maximisation support for people who are financially excluded and who are living on low incomes. I would like to have seen that in the section of the strategy that talks about debt advice."

She continued by noting that certain groups in particular could benefit from more assistance, to ensure they receive all the income they're entitled to through the benefits system. Ms Undy urged: "Our research suggests that, particularly for people with more complex needs, like mental health problems, having access to an individual-face to face, ideally, or over the telephone-who can give them income maximisation support can be transformational.

‌



"That is a key thing that I think is missing in the strategy, but that we could still go further on. I would like to see more on that."

There are several benefit calculator tools available to help you determine if you're eligible for additional benefits. For instance, there is one available on the Turn2us website.

State pension check

Another benefit worth exploring is your state pension entitlement. The full new state pension currently provides £241.30 weekly.

‌



Payments increased by 4.8 per cent in April due to the triple lock. The policy ensures the state pension rises each April in line with the higher of 2.5 per cent, the rise in average earnings, or inflation.

Your entitlement is built up through your National Insurance (NI) payments. Typically, you require 35 years of NI contributions to receive the full amount.

People can check their projected amount using the state pension forecast tool on the Government website. This tool also indicates whether you can boost your entitlement by voluntarily purchasing more NI contributions.

Article continues below

It's crucial to first check that buying extra contributions will genuinely increase your entitlement before paying for them, as this may not be the case.

News.title: Darlington cop killed pensioner racing through red light on 999 call to baby
News.content:
Darlington cop killed pensioner racing through red light on 999 call to baby

PC Mark Roberts was jailed for speeding through a red light while responding to a 999 call where he smashed into an elderly couple and killed a 74-year-old woman

View 2 Images PC Mark Roberts has been jailed (Image: PA)

A police officer who raced through the streets in response to a call about a choking baby has been jailed after his car crashed into a motorbike and killed a woman.

‌



PC Mark Roberts of Northumbria Police was responding to the grade-one emergency call when his marked car smashed into an elderly couple, Ronald and Muriel Pinkney, as they rode their motorbike in Gateshead, north East, on July 8, 2022.

‌



A court heard how Roberts, from Darlington, was driving at 43mph on the 30mph stretch of road near the MetroCentre. As he approached the lights, he was driving around 25mph when his car crashed into the couple, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

‌



Mrs Pinkney, 74, tragically suffered fatal injuries to her head and neck in the horror smash which occurred on a 30mph stretch of road near the MetroCentre. Mr Pinkney also sustained injuries, including a bleed on the brain and several fractures.

The cop has since been prosecuted and convicted of of causing death by dangerous driving and causing serious injury by dangerous driving, Birmingham Live reports, despite a plea from the couple's daughter not to send him to prison.

Roberts was arrested after the collision and answered 'no comment' to questions during his police interview but provided a prepared statement.

‌



In it, he said the ambulance service had requested assistance about a choking five-week-old baby, which indicated paramedics did not believe they could get to the patient before police.

Roberts said he took his marked vehicle from Whickham police station, activated his blue lights and sirens, changing the tone of the alert at times, as he made his way through traffic and red lights.

View 2 Images The cop said he was 'heartbroken' by the tragedy (Image: PA)

‌



Moments before the collision, the officer saw a white van make an emergency stop. He said: "I couldn't see anything else before travelling towards the junction. The next thing I recall is there was a bang and both airbags deployed and I hit the windscreen, which knocked me out for a few seconds."

He he then saw two people on the ground with crash helmets on. Roberts blacked out again and was treated in an ambulance and then taken to hospital. He said: "I believe this was a tragic accident."

Jurors were told Northumbria Police's roadcraft guidance stated that risk taking, even in a 'noble cause', was not justified. In mitigation, the court heard Roberts was 'heartbroken' by the ordeal.

‌



The court was told he had led a 'remarkable life of public service', joining the police after an Army career which saw him serve in Yugoslavia, Afghanistan and Iraq.

He was jailed for two years and three months at Teesside Crown Court on Tuesday (April 7).

Passing sentence, Judge Francis Laird KC, said: "In my judgement only a custodial sentence can be justified for these offences."

‌



The judge told Roberts that he was entitled to use exemptions from the speed limit and the ban on driving through red lights but that 'these exemptions must be exercised cautiously and appropriately'.

"Your speed as you approached the junction was too high," the judge said. "You observed the junction was clear and you simply chose to drive through without stopping or at least reducing your speed to a point where you could stop should another motorist enter the junction."

He went on to say: "The evidence suggests Ronald and Muriel Pinkney were visible to you when you approached the junction, however you were so focused on getting to your destination you failed to notice them."

‌



Roberts was also banned from driving for five years and one month.

The couple's daughter, Dawn Hunter-Pinkney, said in a statement that the family 'don't blame the officer for what happened'.

She said: "For a long time we were angry but the more we hear about why the officer was driving the way he was, the more we understand." She went on to say: "We don't want him to go to prison for doing his job.

‌



"We do accept this is a very tragic accident with a very tragic outcome, but sending the officer to prison won't bring mam back."

Ms Hunter-Pinkney said her parents had been inseparable and her dad had been 'devastated' by his wife's death, going from doing everything with her to 'doing almost nothing'.

She said: "My dad used to be very active and fit, now he rarely leaves the house."

Article continues below

Roberts has been suspended by the force. Andy Hill, assistant chief constable of Northumbria Police, said: "I reiterate my previous comments in recognising that no words will make the pain of Mr Pinkney, his family and anyone impacted by this tragic incident, any easier.

"On behalf of Northumbria Police, I wish to express my sincere condolences for your loss and our thoughts very much continue to be with you at this time." He added: "Each and every day we respond to emergencies and thankfully tragedies of this nature are extremely rare.

"Officers are highly trained and supported to help ensure they keep both themselves and the public safe. Regrettably, on this occasion the standard of driving fell short of what it is expected which has led to the most devastating of outcomes."

News.title: UK weather maps turn bright yellow for 21C scorcher to bake Brits again in days
News.content:
UK weather maps turn bright yellow for 21C scorcher to bake Brits again in days

The UK is expecting warm weather again following the 'mini heatwave' that saw the nation hit a record high for 2026 as temperatures will reach highs of 21C

View 2 Images London is going to be the warmest as the whole nation welcomes warm temperatures (Image: WXCharts )

The UK is set to welcome another sunny spell with temperatures reaching 21C, after the recent 'mini heatwave'.

‌



According to WXCharts weather maps, which use MetDesk data, the hot temperatures are due to hit the nation on Tuesday, April 21.

‌



The south is forecast the warmest temperatures with London expecting to hit a high of 21C at 6pm.

‌



View 2 Images Temperatures will hit 20C on Tuesday (Image: WXCharts)

In the north, temperatures will also near 20C, with Cheshire and Manchester hitting 19C.

‌



In the Midlands the afternoon will see 18C at 12pm and then slightly increase into the evening. In the east the weather will also be scorching.

Even in Scotland there will be highs of 17C, with sunny spells forecast throughout the day.

On April 8, the Met Office announced that temperatures hit a record high for 2026, of 26.5C. After these toasty conditions, temperatures have dropped with chances of snow and rain across much of the UK.

Article continues below

Following the mid twenties warmth that hit much of the nation, Jim Dale, a forecaster for British Weather Services, said it won't be long before things get even warmer - with "late spring" likely to see conditions slide up into the 30Cs.

A spokesperson for the Met Office said: "The southeast is likely to be driest and brightest. Later in this period, conditions may become drier and more settled, perhaps more especially in the north or northwest with the south possibly becoming the focus for showers or longer spells of rain.

"Temperatures will likely be near or slightly above average overall."

News.title: 'I took DNA test as a joke with friend but results came back and blew my mind'
News.content:
'I took DNA test as a joke with friend but results came back and blew my mind'

The person decided to take a DNA test "as a joke" with a friend of theirs. But they didn't expect the results to come back and reveal one massive family secret...

View Image Taking a DNA test can reveal a lot about your family's history (Image: Getty Images)

DNA tests can expose a lot about your family's history. But in some instances, it might reveal something quite life-changing, whether it's good or bad.

‌



One person revealed how a joke turned into something a little more when the results came back. They said how a friend of theirs wanted to do an Ancestry DNA test which showed there was 1% of DNA shared with their fiancée. But when they took the test, it was a little bit more interesting than just 1%. Now they shared the experience on social media which garnered a lot of attention since it was posted.

‌



On Reddit, they began: "So I did Ancestry DNA test as a joke with a friend of mine. Her and her fiancée did the DNA test and shared 1% DNA. I took the test and it paired me to my mum's family that I knew but on my dad side it linked me to two first cousins."

‌



It told them they were either first cousins or their aunt and uncle which would mean their dad is sibling with their parents.

The person added: "They told me they had one uncle that I favoured. This blew my mind because all my life I knew someone else to be my dad.

‌



"I spoke with the guy he didn't remember my mum but they went to the same high school and hung around the same area. I sent her younger picture and he remembers her."

Speaking ahead of the DNA test, they revealed the thought of the results coming back left them "nervous". They added: "He wants to be my dad, I still haven't told my mum or the man I thought was my dad."

They also claimed it was certain the man would be their dad.

‌



Then in an update post, the person exclaimed: "Paternity test is back: He's my dad!"

After fearing how the news would go down with their mum, the person claimed she wasn't upset.

They concluded: "She said she always thought it was a possibility that the man I thought was my dad wasn't. I don't even care I'm excited!"

Article continues below

Speaking in the comments section, they replied to others claiming the news "blew their mind".

They continued: "All I keep thinking is how accurate is Ancestry. I really can't believe this is happening to me. He's a really great guy too I would love for him to be apart of my life. So we will see."

Another person gushed: "So happy for you! I discovered my biological father in January from Ancestry by accident and it has been amazing! I thought someone else was my father as well. Good luck on your journey!"

News.title: 'I was a fit and healthy runner then sign in my neck led to scary diagnosis'
News.content:
'I was a fit and healthy runner then sign in my neck led to scary diagnosis'

Abi Sherratt was fit and healthy, running 5k every day, when a friend noticed something that led to a life-changing diagnosis

View 3 Images Abi Sherratt says her diagnosis came 'out of the blue' (Image: The Institute of Cancer Research)

A runner has told how a friend's comment about her neck changed her life with a "scary" diagnosis that came "out of the blue". Abi Sherratt was "fit and healthy" 26-year-old and had even taken part in a challenge to run 5k every day for a month but within days of successfully completing that she was facing a battle for her health that had shown almost no warning signs.

‌



It was only after a friend noticed that she had a swollen neck that Abi, now 27, had it examined and discovered she had cancer. At the age of 26, in February last year, she was diagnosed with papillary thyroid cancer requiring urgent surgery.

‌



Now, with her treatment complete, she is gearing up to run the London Marathon to demonstrate to herself that she remains capable of tackling demanding challenges after her diagnosis. And she is fundraising for The Institute of Cancer Research, London (ICR) – the world-leading research institute and charity - to help discover treatments for others battling the disease.

‌



View 3 Images Abi will be running in the 2026 London Marathon (Image: Getty Images)

She said: "My diagnosis was a huge shock and totally unexpected. I was only 26 years old, fit and healthy, and I did not feel at all unwell.

"In fact, I had just completed a fitness challenge, running 5K every single day of the previous month. Hearing I had cancer was very scary, especially as it was a diagnosis that had come completely out of the blue." Around 4,100 people are diagnosed with thyroid cancer in the UK every year, with papillary thyroid cancer being the most common form. It accounts for roughly four out of five diagnoses - between 3,200 and 3,300 new cases, according to Cancer Research UK figures, reports MyLondon.

‌



Abi, from Tooting, said she was reassured that her type of cancer was highly treatable with a strong chance of a positive outcome, however her recovery proved to be not quite as straightforward as initially anticipated. Having originally been told she would only require a single operation to remove part of her thyroid, she ultimately needed two surgeries as the cancer had advanced further than previously believed.

Her entire thyroid was removed, along with some lymph nodes, followed by a course of radioactive iodine treatment, a form of targeted radiotherapy.

View 3 Images The thyroid gland is found in the neck just in front of the windpipe - or trachea (Image: Getty)

‌



Abi completed her treatment in September and is hopeful that her next scan in May will confirm it has been 100 per cent successful and that the risk of her cancer returning is minimal. She said: "There is no doubt that it has been a tough journey – both physically and mentally.

"But I know that I'm one of the lucky ones, as my type of cancer was highly curable. Knowing that my type of cancer was so treatable made a real difference and gave me hope.

"That's only possible because of research. It's thanks to groundbreaking discoveries like those being made at The Institute of Cancer Research, that treatments are improving, outcomes are getting better and more people can find hope in the face of an unimaginable diagnosis.

‌



"Through my own experience with cancer, I've seen firsthand how important continued progress is for people and families affected. It's been a reminder of how quickly life can change, and how much we all rely on the breakthroughs that come from research, as well as the dedicated people pushing for better treatments."

Abi has chosen to run the London Marathon for The Institute of Cancer Research - not only to prove to herself that this setback won't hold her back, but to help fund the next scientific breakthrough:

"Running a marathon became something I wanted to do, and getting a place this year after a year of health challenges and for a charity making discoveries to defeat cancer, feels incredibly meaningful. It will be a personal physical feat for me, but one that will help me prove to myself that I am well, that I can still take on tough challenges, that my cancer will not define me or hold me back.

‌



"Cancer research is what gave me the reassurance that I would be OK. Even through it was a horrible and scary time, I knew that treatment was there to make me better again.

"I am thrilled to be running as part of #TeamICR and making a contribution by giving back to research. It is a thank you to those who researched my type of cancer in the past and a sign of hope for those patients who don't have it so easy."

Abi is aiming to raise at least £2,500 for The Institute of Cancer Research. Rachael Potter, Sports and Challenge Events Officer at Institute of Cancer Research, London, said: "We're incredibly grateful for the support of Abi and all of our #teamICR runners taking part in this year's London Marathon. Training for a marathon while fundraising is a huge commitment, and we continue to be inspired by the determination and passion shown by our supporters.

‌



"We hope Abi and all our runners feel motivated knowing they are helping to make a real difference for people affected by cancer. Every pound raised helps drive our research forward, and every mile brings us closer to a future where cancer can be defeated." To back Abi and contribute to the ICR's research, visit: Abi's fundraising page.

Symptoms of thyroid cancer

According to the NHS the main symptoms of thyroid cancer include:

a lump in the front, lower part of your neck – the lump usually feels hard, slowly gets bigger and is not painful

a hoarse voice

a sore throat

difficulty swallowing or breathing

pain in the front of your neck, or a feeling like something is pressing against your neck

‌



Other symptoms can include:

a red face (flushing) – this may be harder to see on brown or black skin

softer poos or diarrhoea

weight loss

a cough

The NHS warns: "These symptoms are very common and can be caused by many different conditions. Having them does not definitely mean you have thyroid cancer.

Article continues below

"But it's important to get them checked by a GP. This is because if they're caused by cancer, finding it early may mean it's easier to treat."

News.title: Grandmother's chilling revelation as huge dog kills girl, 19
News.content:
Grandmother's chilling revelation as huge dog kills girl, 19

Jamie Lee Briscoe, 19, was mauled to death by a seven-year-old lurcher, according to one social media user, who said the dog had once 'slept on my granddaughter's bed'

View 2 Images Jamie Lee Briscoe has been named locally as the teen who died following the horror attack (Image: Facebook/ Tina Wells)

A killer dog that mauled a 19-year-old girl to death was a treasured family pet that slept on the bed, a grandmother has revealed, as tributes pour in for the tragic teen.

‌



Jamie Lee Briscoe has been named locally as the teen who died in Leaden Roding, Essex, after sustaining serious injuries in the night time attack by the dog, said to be a lurcher breed. Jamie was found severely injured by Essex Police responding to a 10.45pm call to a property in the area, and pronounced dead at the scene, the service said in a statement.

‌



Devastated friends and family members have offered tributes following the horror incident, including one nan who revealed the dog in question once slept on her granddaughter's bed.

‌



View 2 Images Police confirmed that Jamie died on the scene following the dog attack (Image: East Anglia News Service)

One relative wrote in a post on Facebook : "Our darling Jamie-Lea rip our girl." Tina Wells, another poster, identified the dog as a "seven-year-old lurcher" and "family pet". Ms Wells revealed that the dog had "slept on my granddaughter's bed", adding: "It's devastating."

Another neighbour added that the shock incident was "really tragic" while remembering Jamie, who they said was "well-liked by the kids".

‌



They said: "It's really tragic. I feel for the whole family. She was well-liked by the kids. We didn't know what happened until this morning. For all concerned, it's devastating.

"We feel for the family. We're still trying to process it. It has been a shock." Another added: "They kept themselves to themselves, they never caused us any problems. It's just very, very sad and very tragic."

Essex Police said in a statement that a 37-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of being in charge of a dog dangerously out of control causing injury resulting in death following the Dunmow incident. Essex Assistant Chief Constable Stuart Hooper said: “I know this incident will be a shock to the local community.

Article continues below

"My thoughts, and those of us all at Essex Police, are with the loved ones of the woman who died yesterday. We will have officers in the area throughout today so please come and speak to them if you have any information or have any concerns.

"Experienced detectives are leading the investigation to understand exactly what has happened.” The service has launched an appeal for information as enquiries continue, with members of the public encouraged to get in touch with Essex Police if they have information, CCTV, dashcam or other footage that could assist police.

People who believe they have pertinent information have been asked to get in touch via the service's online portal or the 101 police non-emergency number, quoting incident 1419 of 10 April.

News.title: New row as locals fume at Kate Middleton's sister after sudden closure on estate
News.content:
New row as locals fume at Kate Middleton's sister after sudden closure on estate

Fury grows as locals clash with James Matthews and Pippa Middleton over a blocked Berkshire footpath, with safety fears rising and campaigners warning it's part of a wider access crisis

View 5 Images Kate's sister Pippa is at the centre of a local dispute (Image: Alamy Stock Photo)

A bitter row is brewing in the Berkshire countryside, and this time, it's a royal-adjacent dispute that's left locals fuming.

‌



Residents in the village of Kintbury have hit out after a long-used walking route was suddenly shut off near a luxury estate owned by James Matthews - the husband of Pippa Middleton and brother-in-law to Catherine, Princess of Wales.

‌



At the heart of the dispute is Mill Lane, a quiet access route locals say they've used for decades to reach nearby footpaths, the village centre and St Mary's Church. The lane runs alongside the sprawling Barton Court Estate - a £15 million property featuring a 32-room Georgian mansion and more than 100 acres of land on the banks of the River Kennet.

‌



Kate Middleton gets huge boost after sad family burden as she lays down strict rules READ MORE :

View 5 Images Pippa Middleton and James Matthews married in 2017 (Image: Getty)

But tensions flared after the couple reportedly installed electric gates shortly after buying the estate in 2022, blocking off access to the lane. Warning signs soon followed, declaring the route private and off-limits to the public.

In 2024, James, 50, submitted a highway declaration notice stating that Mill Lane was not accessible to the public.

‌



For residents, the impact has resulted in potentially dangerous walking routes to get around the lane closure. Locals claim the closure has forced walkers onto a narrow country road with no pavement, raising serious safety concerns.

Local Neil G Lawrence said: "I was always of the belief that this route off of Station Road to the Kintbury footpath was public. When planning a walk, and executing a walk, the route looks logical, both on any available map and in reality on the ground."

View 5 Images The property is worth a staggering £15million (Image: Alamy Stock Photo)

‌



Campaigners say the route had long provided a safer alternative, allowing villagers to avoid road traffic while travelling between key parts of the community.

Eugene Futcher, chairman of West Berkshire Ramblers, has warned that removing access puts people "at risk", insisting the path has been used regularly for generations.

The dispute has now escalated into a formal battle over public access rights.

‌



Campaigners argue that because the route has been used openly for more than 20 years, it should legally be recognised as a public right of way. However, that decision is currently under appeal, with the final outcome expected to be determined by the Planning Inspectorate.

View 5 Images James Matthews, a multi-millionaire, bought the estate in 2022 (Image: Getty)

The controversy has also drawn wider attention from walking charity The Ramblers.

‌



Sophie Redmond, Programme Manager for Paths, said the situation reflects a broader national issue. She explained that "thousands of miles of local paths are missing, blocked or unusable," preventing people from accessing routes they are legally entitled to use.

Pointing specifically to Mill Lane, she added that evidence shows it has been walked by the community "for over 20 years without interruption," meaning the public should have the right to continue using it.

She warned the closure has forced residents onto a "busy road with no pedestrian path," highlighting the real-world consequences of losing access.

‌



While neither James or Pippa has publicly commented, some locals believe the closure may be linked to privacy concerns following the estate's purchase five years after the pair wed.

Feelings in the village are said to be running high. Testimonies heard by Kintbury Parish Council revealed a divide, with some residents saying they avoided the lane in the past due to signage, while others maintained it had been used freely for years.

Despite this, the council ultimately backed its designation as a right of way. According to Redmond, the row in Berkshire is far from unique.

‌



Across Britain, access to local green spaces is becoming increasingly restricted - with blocked paths disproportionately affecting less affluent communities.

View 5 Images Signs and gates were put up when the couple moved into the estate (Image: Getty)

"This isn't just unfair, it's unhealthy," she said, warning that reduced access to nature is deepening inequalities in health and wellbeing.

‌



The Ramblers' Access Denied campaign is now calling for stronger protections and expanded walking networks to ensure communities can safely reach green spaces.

Eugene Futcher, chairman of West Berkshire Ramblers, claims residents have enjoyed "unfettered access" to the lane since the 1960s. Speaking to The Times, he stated: "It is a safe way to get to and from the village, so walkers are put at risk if they have to use the road."

The Barton Court estate has been contacted for a comment.

News.title: Queen's best friend played cruel prank on her and was told 'you're sacked'
News.content:
Queen's best friend played cruel prank on her and was told 'you're sacked'

Angela Kelly bought the Queen a sweet gift during a Royal Tour to Australia - but she decided to have a bit of fun with it first at Her Majesty's expense

View 4 Images The late Queen (Image: Getty Images)

The centenary of the birth of the late Queen is being celebrated with the biggest-ever exhibition of her incredible wardrobe. And the show features designs by the woman, who once described herself as the former monarch's 'best friend'.

‌



Angela Kelly, was the former monarch's personal dresser and designed many of her most memorable and colourful outfits - and was one of her most trusted aides. The pair were said to chat about "anything and everything”, as they drank tea and swapped jokes and anecdotes about their grandchildren. Ms Kelly released two books with her former boss's blessing about her life curating her wardrobe, designing her vibrant looks and looking after her jewellery.

‌



William and Kate lead the royals in huge show of unity as they celebrate Easter READ MORE :

View 4 Images The late Queen at London Fashion Week with Dame Anna Wintour and Angela Kelly in 2018 (Image: Getty Images)

‌



And in one of her books, she revealed the prank she played on the late Queen during a royal tour of Australia in 2006 - and Her Majesty's witty response to it.

Writing in her book The Other Side of the Coin, the dresser explained that thelate Queen was desperate to see a kookaburra while Down Under. Unfortunately, she had trouble spotting one, but Ms Kelly saw a cute cuddly toy version at a Sydney market and decided to buy it and give it to her - but not before a little fun first.

She writes: "I had something in mind I thought the Queen would enjoy." When she got back to Governor's House, where they were all staying, she placed the toy in a little cage on the balcony outside her room. She then told the then monarch she had spotted a "funny-looking grey bird" through the window.

‌



Ms Kelly added: "The Queen looked outside and shouted 'It's a kookaburra!' I went to open the cage doors and she said loudly 'No! Don't do that! It will fly away!' and was behind me in a flash. Turning to her Majesty while trying to keep a straight face, I solemnly told her it was dead." The Queen looked "horrified" until her dresser walked towards her with outstretched arms and said "April Fool".

View 4 Images Ms Kelly worked for the late Queen for almost 30 years (Image: PA)

She explained: "She had only two words for me: "You're sacked. I was laughing uncontrollably as Her Majesty turned to His Royal Highness and said "Do you know what she has just done to me? Angela has had me!".

‌



The late Queen is said to have taken the little toy back to Windsor Castle with her, where it lived on the back of the sofa in her private living room.

Since Elizabeth II's death, Ms Kelly has lost her grace-and-favour home on the Windsor estate and told her followers on Instagram : "Getting ready to say goodbye. I am moving at last to my new home which I will be able to call My Home at last." Replying to a friend, she said her work phone had been disconnected and added she'd be moving to the Peak District, close to Sheffield, in a house provided by the King.

This week, six of Ms Kelly's outfits that she created for her former boss went on show in an exhibition at Buckingham Palace called Queen Elizabeth II: Her Life in Style, although she has had little contact with the Palace since her departure.

‌



View 4 Images Ms Kelly at the late Queen's state funeral (Image: Getty Images)

However, as the 100th anniversary of the late Queen's birth approaches the 68-year-old told Vanity Fair, how she remembers dancing and singing along to ABBA's Dancing Queen in her bedroom.

She explained: "Every morning the queen would listen to the Terry Wogan show on Radio 2. When the song Dancing Queen came on she loved it, and both of us would dance. The Queen would move from side to side and sing.

‌



"Her Majesty loved singing and had a good voice. I didn’t. I’d get carried away and be dancing all round her like I was at a disco, and the queen would tell me to 'move over' because I can’t sing and we laughed. They were moments to cherish, to see the queen so relaxed."

She also reminisced about spending the Easter holidays with the late Queen at Windsor adding: "The family would visit and she loved being granny. Her Majesty took her great-grandchildren out riding or walking. She did barbecues and fun things and she always washed the dishes, even when she was entertaining the prime minister.

Article continues below

“It was just a normal loving family, to be quite honest. If the duke, or whoever was cooking, burnt the burgers she’d just laugh. As long as they had extra to put back on, and as long as all the family were fed and watered, that was all right. The Queen was just full of energy and a really cool granny, to be honest."

News.title: Grand National 2026: I Am Maximus becomes two-time winner
News.content:
I Am Maximus became the first horse since Red Rum in 1977 to regain the Grand National as trainer Willie Mullins celebrated his third consecutive victory in the race at Aintree.

The 2024 winner and last year's runner-up came into the race as the 9-2 favourite and backed that up by finishing ahead of Iroko, Jordans and Johnnywho.

It made Irishman Mullins, who won the race for a fourth time in total, the first trainer since Vincent O'Brien between 1953 and 1955 to win in three successive years.

The feat means that JP McManus is now the leading owner in the history of the race with four wins - backing up the victories of Don't Push It in 2010, Minella Times in 2021 and I Am Maximus in 2024.

McManus could also boast owning three of the top four in Saturday's showpiece race, with only Jordans not in his stable.

Red Rum's second and third victories came in 1974 and 1977, and I Am Maximus is the first horse to have won the race in non-consecutive years since.

Further history for I Am Maximus was made by him, with a handicap of 11st 12lbs, becoming the first top weight to win since Red Rum carried 12 stone to victory in 1974.

Jockey Paul Townend said he felt "privileged" to be riding I Am Maximus.

He told ITV: "He's tough. He's a really, really good horse, and although Grangeclare West and Nick Rockett looked good in training, this lad wasn't telling me not to ride him.

"He is so good and has such an engine. He will gallop to the end of the world for you. I am really privileged. What a horse.

"Grand Nationals and Gold Cups are the pinnacle of the sport and I have them both."

The article below is an excerpt from my newsletter: Well Enough with Harry Bullmore. To get my latest thoughts on fitness and wellbeing pop your email address into the box above to get the newsletter direct to your inbox.

I spent some time away from my desk last month and returned to a four-figure avalanche of unread emails. After spending two days wrangling my inbox into submission, I found myself feeling uncharacteristically frustrated.

There were plenty of great messages in there, but they were drowned out by subject lines covering “Pilates arms” as a status symbol, the hottest fitness trends of 2026, recovery protocols, and how to hack your body for better health.

My problem with these emails is that fitness is quite possibly the least trendy thing on earth, or at least it should be. It’s not built by constantly following the latest fad, but rather by consistently doing healthy things as often as you can.

A workout doesn’t become any more or less effective just because everyone is talking about it. There’s nothing wrong with trying something new to keep things fresh, but the stuff that works has always worked, and it will continue to do so.

The human body is something of a black box – there’s a lot we don’t know about it. But there are certain behaviours we can label as beneficial with a decent degree of confidence: moving regularly, eating fruits and vegetables and sleeping well are, arguably, the big three.

Recent research from the University of Sydney studied almost 60,000 people with a median age of 64 to find out how much they needed to change their diet, exercise and sleep routines to have a meaningful impact on their health.

The results were surprisingly achievable, particularly for those currently performing poorly in these three areas. For this group, an increase of just 15 minutes of sleep, 1.6 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise and half a serving of vegetables each day was associated with a 10 per cent lower risk of death.

Are these changes trendy? No. But are they effective? Apparently so, if done consistently and in conjunction with one another.

“We understand that making major behavioural changes on a large scale is very complex, and if you set the bar too high – such as telling people to make drastic changes to their diet, sleep for an extra hour every night or go to the gym five times per week – they may be less likely to succeed,” lead author Professor Emmanuel Stamatakis tells me.

“Our work is not about guilt-triggered behavioural change, it’s about supporting people to make whatever degree of change they can in the long term.”

Another interview I enjoyed this week also appears to support my (admittedly, fairly mild-mannered) tirade against health trends. Pain scientist and Tell Me Where It Hurts author Dr Rachel Zoffness told me that chronic pain is widely misunderstood and mistreated, and presented an intuitive alternative.

She says people usually focus on the area that hurts and the physical symptoms, but these are only part of the puzzle.

“The brain receives data from the injured body part, of course, but also from our emotions, social health and environment,” Dr Zoffness tells me, “we all know our bodies hurt more when we’re stressed, anxious or depressed.”

Everyone has things that make their pain feel worse, such as stressful days, poor sleep and even bad weather – a cocktail she describes as a “high pain recipe”. By default, then, everyone must also have a “low pain recipe”, or things that ease their pain.

What are the ingredients of a low pain recipe? You guessed it. For the most part, they are consistent, health-promoting behaviours such as managing your stress levels, spending time outdoors and socialising, alongside the obvious sleep, diet and exercise factors.

And finally this week, I wanted to hone in on the exercise element and share a recent chat I had with Marchon Victoria head coach Paddy James about the most efficient way to build full-body muscle.

Many people assume that, to achieve this, you need to sacrifice an hour each day. But in Paddy’s considerable experience, two weekly full-body strength training sessions, each lasting no more than 45 minutes, are enough for most people to see impressive results. This approach is also far easier to stay consistent with – and consistency is the key to a lasting uptick in your health and fitness.

That brings us to our weekly conclusion: what thread connects this trio of pieces? It’s certainly not trendiness or flashy, buzzworthy advice. Instead, they all champion basic healthy behaviours, done consistently. Better yet, they suggest that a couple of small positive changes can go a long way in improving your health.

News.title: Can Hungary’s opposition finally topple Europe’s most pro-Russian leader?
News.content:
The most important election in Europe for a long time is taking place in Hungary on Sunday, April 12.

After 16 years in power, Europe's longest-serving leader Viktor Orbán is seeking re-election in a de facto vote on the future direction of Hungary: toward European-style liberal democracy or closer ties with Russia.

Orbán is the most pro-Russian leader in the EU, and his defeat would be a significant blow to Putin, Trump and the international populist movement.

Opposition leader Péter Magyar has built his campaign on promises to restore Hungary's Western orientation towards the EU and Nato.

Going into the final week of the election, most opinion polls put Magyar and his opposition Tisza party ahead of Orbán’s Fidesz party.

But JD Vance’s trip to Budapest this week, offering Orbán’s campaign a last-minute boost from the Trump administration, might be enough to turn the tide in favour of Fidesz.

For a factory worker in Haiti, the war in distant Iran means he now has to walk two hours to work and the same distance home each day, because he can no longer afford public transportation.

On a recent morning, Alexandre Joseph, 35, fretted about his family’s future in a loud voice, attracting the attention of passersby in Port-au-Prince, Haiti’s capital.

“The government raised the prices of gasoline, diesel and kerosene, hitting my family. I now am unable to feed my two children on the salary I have,” he said.

The conflict in Iran has caused oil prices in Haiti to surge, disrupting critical supply chains, doubling transportation costs and forcing millions of undernourished people to cut back on already scarce meals.

Haiti, the most impoverished country in the Western Hemisphere, has been hit the hardest by rising oil prices that experts warn will deepen a spiraling humanitarian crisis.

‘One of the most fragile countries in the world’

On April 2, Haiti’s government announced a 37% increase in the cost of diesel and a 29% increase in the cost of gasoline.

“The consequences are huge,” said Erwan Rumen, deputy country director for the United Nations World Food Program in Haiti. “It’s one of the most fragile countries in the world.”

Almost half of Haiti's nearly 12 million inhabitants already face high levels of acute food insecurity. In recent months, Rumen noted, about 200,000 people dropped from the emergency phase to the acute one, a significant milestone.

“What is a bit frightening is to see that so many efforts could be basically wiped out by things that are completely out of our control,” he said. “This part of the population is extremely fragile. They’re on the verge of collapsing completely.”

Gang violence has exacerbated hunger, with armed men controlling key roads and disrupting the transportation of goods. An increase in food prices will only worsen hunger in a country where gangs easily recruit children whose families need food and money.

Emmline Toussaint, main coordinator of Mary’s Meals' BND school-feeding program in Haiti, said that gas stations in some regions are selling fuel 25% to 30% higher than even what the government stipulated because of gang violence and difficulties with trucks trying to access certain areas.

She said the U.S.-based nonprofit is forced to use boats and take longer and multiple roads to feed the 196,000 children they serve across Haiti to avoid armed groups.

“The humanitarian crisis that we’re facing right now is at its worst,” she said. “So far, we are doing our best not to step back. Now, more than ever, the kids need us. … Most of them, it’s the only meal they receive.”

‘Everything will go up’

Fedline Jean-Pierre, a soft-spoken mother of a 7-year-old boy, sat under the shade of a tattered beach umbrella as she mulled increasing the prices of carrots, tomatoes and other produce she sells at an outdoor market in Port-au-Prince.

“People are not buying now because they don’t have money,” she said, noting she likely won’t have a choice but to increase prices to survive. “I have a child to feed.”

The 35-year-old mother said she and her son have lived for two years in a cramped and unsanitary shelter, among the record 1.4 million Haitians displaced by gang violence in recent years.

“The government doesn’t do anything for me,” she said. “Gas is up now, meaning everything will go up.”

Street vendor Maxime Poulard buys charcoal from suppliers to resell at a higher price. Occasionally he sells two bags of charcoal a day, but he thinks he soon will only be able to afford to buy half a bag to resell.

“Traveling is expensive; eating is expensive; everything is expensive,” he said. “I’m not sure if I will be able to hold on much more.”

Nearly 40% of Haitians are surviving on less than $2.15 a day, according to the World Bank. Meanwhile, Haiti’s economy contracted for the seventh consecutive year, with inflation reaching 32% at the end of fiscal year 2025.

Joseph, the factory worker, said he plans to sell soft drinks at night out of his home to try and earn more money, but even then, that won't be enough: “We’re also going to reduce the way we normally eat.”

‘Impossible tradeoffs’

On April 6, Haitians dragged burning tires and other debris to block streets and protest the increase in fuel prices in Port-au-Prince, of which an estimated 90% is controlled by gangs.

Local media reported gunfire as some Haitians forced the drivers of small colorful buses known as tap-taps to disembark their passengers.

Marc Jean-Louis, a 29-year-old tap-tap driver, said passengers are increasingly bartering fares, but he can't afford to offer discounts.

“All the money is going toward gas,” he said as he called on the government to reduced prices “so that everyone can breathe.”

Haitians fear more violence as the country’s poverty and hunger deepens.

Rumen, with the U.N.’s World Food Program, said they’ve been unable to reach 60,000 people in Haiti’s central region who are awaiting aid. A powerful gang recently attacked the area, killing more than 70 people, according to the U.N.

“We're going to have more needs and less resources,” he warned.

Allen Joseph, program manager for Mercy Corps in Haiti, said rising oil prices are crushing the country’s fragile economy: “The families already spending most of their income on food will face impossible tradeoffs.”

He warned the increase will affect access to basic services, including potable water.

“This is not an abstract inflation,” he warned. “It will directly impact survival.”

___

Coto reported from San Juan, Puerto Rico.
